## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92539.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92539.3.sa1)

Summary:

The authors conducted two tasks at 300 days separation. First, a social perception task, where Ps responded whether a pictured person either deserved or needed help. Second, an altruism task, where Ps are offered monetary allocations for themselves and a partner. Ps decide whether to accept, or a default allocation of 20 dollars each. The partners differed in perceived merit, such that they were highly deserving, undeserving or unknown. This categorisation was decided on the basis of a prisoners dilemma game the partner played beforehand. "Need" was also manipulated, by altering the probability that the partner must have their hand in cold water at the end of the experiment and this partner can use the money to buy themselves out. These two tasks were conducted to assess the perception of need/merit in the first instance, and how this relates to social behaviour in the second. fMRI data were collected alongside behavioural.

The authors present many analyses of behaviour (including DDM results) and fMRI. E.g., they demonstrate that they could decode across the mentalising network whether someone was making a need or deserving judgement vs control judgements but couldn't decode need vs deserving. And that brain responses during merit inferences (merit - control) systematically covaried with participants' merit sensitivity scores in the rTPJ. They also found relationships between behaviour and rTPJ in the altruism task. And that merit sensitivity in the perception task predicted influence of merit on social behaviour in the altruism task.

Strengths:

This manuscript represents a sensible model to predict social perceptions and behaviours, and a tidy study design with interesting findings. The introduction introduced the field especially brilliantly for a general audience.

Weaknesses:

These are small samples. This is especially the case for the correlational questions. The limitation is acknowledged, but does mean that we cannot conclude much from absent relationships, where the likelihood of Type II error is high.

Decoding analyses. The authors decode need vs merit, and need+merit vs control, not the content of these inferences. The logic of these analyses implies that there is a distributed representation of merit that does not relate to its content but is an abstracted version that applies to all merit judgements. However, these analyses are not central to the authors' aims and conclusions, so this is just a minor point.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92539.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92539.3.sa2)

When people help others is an important psychological and neuroscientific question. It has received much attention from the psychological side, but comparatively less from neuroscience. The paper translates some ideas from a social Psychology domain to neuroscience using a neuroeconomically oriented computational approach. In particular, the paper is concerned with the idea that people help others based on perceptions of merit/deservingness, but also because they require/need help. To this end, the authors conduct two experiments with an overlapping participant pool:

(1) A social perception task in which people see images of people that have previously been rated on merit and need scales by other participants. In a blockwise fashion, people decide to whether the depicted person (a) deserves help, (b) needs help, and (c) whether the person uses both hands (== control condition)

(2) In an altruism task, people make costly helping decisions by deciding between giving a certain amount of money to themselves or another person. It is manipulated how much the other person needs and deserves the money.

The authors use sound and robust computational modelling approach for both tasks using evidence accumulation models. They analyse behavioural data for both tasks, showing that the behaviour is indeed influenced, as expected, by the deservingness and the need of the shown people. Neurally, the authors use a block-wise analysis approach to find differences in activity levels across conditions of the social perception task. The authors do find large activation clusters in areas related to theory of mind. Interestingly, they also find that activity in TPJ that relates to the deservingness condition correlates with people's deservingness ratings while they do the task, but also with computational parameters related to helping others in the second task, the one that was conducted many months later. Also some behavioural parameters correlate across the two tasks, suggesting that how deserving of help others are perceived reflects a relatively stable feature that translates into concrete helping decisions later-on.

The conclusions of the paper are overall well supported by the data.

(1) I found that the modelling was done very thoroughly for both tasks. Overall, I had the impression that the methods are very solid with many supplementary analyses. The computational modelling is done very well.

(2) A slight caveat, however, regarding this aspect, is that, in my view, the tasks are relatively simplistic, so that even the complex computational models do not as much as they can in the case of more complex paradigms. For example, the bias term in the model seems to correspond to the mean response rate in a very direct way (please correct me if I am wrong).

(3) Related to the simple tasks: The fMRI data is analysed in a simple block-fashion. This is in my view not appropriate to discern the more subtle neural substrates of merit/need-based decision making or person perception. Correspondingly, the neural activation patterns (merit > control, need > control) are relatively broad and unspecific. They do not seem to differ in the classic theory of mind regions, that are the focus of the analyses.

(4) However, the relationship between neural signal and behavioural merit sensitivity in TPJ is noteworthy.

(5) The latter is even more the case, as the neural signal and aspects of the behaviour are correlated across subjects with the second task that is conducted much later. Such a correlation is very impressive and suggests that the tasks are sensitive for important individual differences in helping perception/behaviour.

(6) That being said, the number of participants in the latter analyses are at the lower end of the number of participants that are these days used for across-participant correlations.

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92539.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92539.3.sa3)

Summary:

The paper aims at providing a neurocomputational account on how social perception translates in prosocial behaviors. Participants first completed a novel social perception task during fMRI scanning, in which were asked to judge the merit or need of people depicted in different situations. Second , a separate altruistic choice task was used to examine how the perception of merit and need influences the weights people place on themselves, others and fairness when deciding to provide help. Finally, a link between perception and action was drawn in those participants who completed both tasks.

Strengths:

The paper is overall very well written and presented, leaving the reader at ease when describing complex methods and results. The approach used by the author is very compelling, as it combines computational modeling of behavior and neuroimaging data analyses. Despite not being able to comment on the computational model, I find the approach used (to disentangle sensitivity and biases, for merit and need) very well described and derived from previous theoretical work. Results are also clearly described and interpreted.

Weaknesses:

In the social perception task, merit and need are evaluated by means of very different cues that rely on different cognitive processes (more abstract thinking for merit than need). Despite this limitation of the task, the authors were able to argue convincingly in the revised version about the solidity of their findings. Sample size is quite small for study 2, nevertheless the results provide convincing evidence.

results.result: Both merit and need perceptions recruited the brain's mentalizing network to a similar extent, with no significant differences in activation patterns between the two types of judgments. The medial prefrontal cortex, superior temporal sulcus, temporal pole, temporoparietal junction, and posterior cingulate cortex were activated during both merit and need inferences. Multivariate decoding analyses failed to distinguish between merit and need judgments, suggesting common neural codes for both types of social perceptual judgments supported by general-purpose rather than domain-specific mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C24, and C61-C63 collectively demonstrate that merit and need perceptions engage overlapping neural circuitry. The fMRI data (C2, C21, C22) show activation in the mentalizing network for both conditions, univariate analyses (C23, C24) reveal minimal differences, and multivariate pattern analyses (C61, C62) fail to decode the judgment type. These converging lines of evidence strongly support the conclusion that both judgments rely on general-purpose social cognitive mechanisms (C63).

results.result: A computational model of social perception identified two independent mechanisms underlying individual differences in social judgments: perceptual bias (tendency to perceive others as meritorious/needy) and perceptual sensitivity (ability to discriminate based on normative evidence). Participants showed positive sensitivity for merit, need, and control judgments, a positive merit bias, and a negative need bias. Bias and sensitivity parameters were uncorrelated for both merit and need judgments, though merit and need bias were positively correlated.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C14-C20, and C64 provide strong computational and statistical support for the dual-mechanism model. The model adequately fits the data (C64), sensitivity parameters are significantly positive (C14), bias parameters show expected patterns (C15, C16), and the independence of bias and sensitivity is demonstrated through correlation analyses (C17, C18, C19). The correlation between merit and need bias (C20) adds nuance without contradicting the main finding of independent mechanisms.

results.result: Individual differences in merit sensitivity (from the computational model) were associated with activation in the right temporoparietal junction (rTPJ) during merit perceptions. Participants with higher merit sensitivity scores exhibited larger rTPJ responses when appraising someone's merit, and this neural signature was linked to context-sensitive changes in altruistic behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C25 and C26 provide direct fMRI evidence for the brain-behavior relationship, showing that rTPJ activation during merit judgments correlates with computational estimates of merit sensitivity. Claim C7 extends this finding by linking rTPJ activation to behavioral outcomes in the altruism task. The statistical thresholds are appropriate (p < 0.001 voxel-level, FWE cluster-corrected p < 0.05), and the finding is replicated in the reduced sample (n=25).

results.result: In the altruism task, participants' generosity was independently influenced by both partner merit and partner need, with no significant interaction between these factors. Participants were more generous to high (vs. low) merit partners, unknown (vs. low) merit partners, and high (vs. low) need partners. Merit-induced and need-induced changes in generosity were uncorrelated across individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 and C67-C68 provide converging evidence from mixed-effects logistic regression showing independent main effects of merit and need on generosity. The lack of significant interactions (C31, C68) and the absence of correlation between merit- and need-induced changes (C33) strongly support the independence of these two factors. The statistical analyses are appropriate with adequate sample size (n=28) and proper corrections for multiple comparisons.

results.result: A computational model of altruistic choice revealed that self-related outcomes primarily guided decisions, but partner merit and need systematically altered the weights on self-regard, other-regard, and fairness considerations. High (vs. low) merit partners decreased self-regard weights while increasing other-regard and fairness weights. High (vs. low) need partners decreased self-regard weights and increased other-regard weights but decreased fairness weights.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 describe the computational mechanisms by which merit and need influence altruistic decisions, supported by a well-fitting model (C65, C66: R²=0.33, significantly better than null). The pattern of weight changes is internally consistent and statistically significant (all p's < 0.01, FDR corrected). The differential effect on fairness weights (increased for merit, decreased for need) provides mechanistic insight into how these factors operate.

results.result: Individual differences in merit sensitivity from the social perception task predicted merit-related changes in generosity in the altruism task completed months later (r=0.51, p=0.010). This relationship was mediated by changes in other-regard and self-regard weights during altruistic decision-making, with individuals showing higher merit sensitivity exhibiting greater discrimination in generosity toward high versus low merit partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C40, C6, and C69 demonstrate a stable perception-action link across time (average 303 days). The correlation between merit sensitivity and behavioral changes is statistically significant (C40), and follow-up analyses identify the specific computational mechanisms (changes in other-regard and self-regard weights, C6). The effect size (r=0.51) is substantial given the temporal separation and different task contexts.

results.result: Individual differences in merit bias from the social perception task predicted context-independent overall other-regard during altruistic choice. People who tended to perceive others as deserving showed higher weights on others' benefits across all conditions in the altruism task completed approximately 10 months later.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C70, and C71 establish a link between perceptual bias and general prosocial orientation. The correlation between merit bias and overall other-regard (C70: r=0.50, p=0.035, FDR corrected) demonstrates temporal stability of individual differences. However, the absence of a direct correlation with overall generosity (mentioned in text, p=0.282) suggests the relationship operates through specific computational mechanisms (other-regard weights) rather than overall behavior.

results.result: Both merit sensitivity and rTPJ activation during merit perceptions independently predicted changes in other-regard during altruistic choice approximately 10 months later. Neural responses in the rTPJ provided predictive information about context-dependent changes in prosocial behavior above and beyond behavioral measures of merit sensitivity alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, and C72 demonstrate that neural measures add predictive value beyond behavioral measures. The regression analysis (C43) shows both merit sensitivity (β=0.20, p=0.021) and rTPJ activation (β=0.29, p=0.029) independently predict behavioral changes, with substantial total explanatory power (R²=0.40). This supports the notion of stable, biologically-based individual differences in social perception.

results.result: Individual differences in need sensitivity from the social perception task did not predict need-induced changes in generosity in the altruism task.
results.evaluation: Claim C27 reports a null finding (p=0.745) for the relationship between need sensitivity and behavioral changes. While the authors acknowledge this limitation and suggest it may be due to small sample size (n=25 overlap), the absence of effects for need across multiple analyses (sensitivity, bias, neural correlates) raises questions about whether the null result reflects true absence of effect, insufficient power, or methodological limitations in measuring need-related processes.

results.result: The study included 44 participants in the social perception task and 28 participants in the altruism task, with 25 participants completing both tasks separated by an average of 303 days (range: 27-663 days). Participants showed substantial individual variability in their perceptions of merit (33-81% yes responses) and need (28-73% yes responses).
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C13, and C45-C50 provide clear methodological details about sample sizes, exclusion criteria, and temporal separation between tasks. The reported ranges of perceptual responses (C12, C13) demonstrate meaningful individual differences. However, the relatively small final sample sizes (n=28 for altruism task, n=25 for overlap) and substantial attrition may limit statistical power for detecting some effects, particularly for need-related analyses.

results.result: The study employed appropriate experimental procedures including incentive-compatible payment, normative ratings from an independent sample, controlled stimulus presentation timing, and manipulation of partner merit and need across multiple trials. Participants experienced the painful cold pressor task themselves to ensure salience of the need manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C60 describe methodological details that support the validity of the experimental manipulations. The incentive-compatible payment structure (C51), use of an independent normative sample (C52), controlled timing parameters (C53-C55), adequate trial numbers (C56), appropriate monetary ranges (C57), and personal experience with the CPT (C58) all contribute to experimental rigor. The fMRI acquisition parameters (C59, C60) are standard for this type of research.

results.result: The findings point toward stable, biologically-based individual differences in perceptual processes related to abstract social concepts like merit, with potential implications for favoritism or discrimination in social settings.
results.evaluation: Claims C73 and C74 represent broad interpretive conclusions that extend beyond the direct evidence. While the temporal stability (10 months) and neural correlates support the notion of stable individual differences (C73), the claim about 'biologically-based' mechanisms requires caution given the correlational nature of fMRI data. The speculation about implications for favoritism and discrimination (C74) is reasonable but not directly tested in this study and would require additional research in real-world contexts.

results.result: People selectively help others based on perceptions of their merit or need, being more likely to assist those in need and withhold aid from those perceived as undeserving. The need principle involves distributing resources to those requiring them regardless of deservingness, while the merit principle focuses on allocating resources based on deservingness irrespective of actual need.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C11 establish the theoretical foundation and prior literature context for the study. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established research (C8, C9) and represent standard definitions in moral philosophy (C10, C11). However, these are primarily background claims rather than novel findings from the current study.

results.result: Merit and need perceptions both recruited the brain's mentalizing network (mPFC, STS, temporal pole, TPJ, PCC), with no significant differences between merit and need inferences in these regions. Need inferences showed greater activation in cuneus, intraparietal sulcus, and sensorimotor cortex. Multivariate decoding could not distinguish need from merit inferences, suggesting common neural codes for both types of social perceptual judgments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledged these findings, with one noting 'they demonstrate that they could decode across the mentalising network whether someone was making a need or deserving judgement vs control judgements but couldn't decode need vs deserving.' Another reviewer noted the findings show 'large activation clusters in areas related to theory of mind.' The lack of decoding between need and merit was treated as a minor point about interpretation rather than a critique of the findings themselves.

results.result: A computational model identified two independent mechanisms underlying social perceptions: bias (tendency to perceive others as meritorious/needy) and sensitivity (propensity to sample and integrate evidence). Participants showed positive merit bias, negative need bias, and positive sensitivity parameters for merit, need, and control. Bias and sensitivity were uncorrelated within merit and need judgments, but merit and need biases were correlated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the computational modeling approach, with one stating 'the modelling was done very thoroughly for both tasks' and 'the computational modelling is done very well.' Another noted 'the approach used by the author is very compelling, as it combines computational modeling of behavior and neuroimaging data analyses.' One reviewer raised a minor caveat that 'the tasks are relatively simplistic' and the bias term may correspond directly to mean response rate, but this did not undermine acceptance of the findings.

results.result: Brain responses during merit inferences systematically covaried with participants' merit sensitivity scores in the right temporoparietal junction (rTPJ). Participants with larger merit sensitivity scores exhibited larger rTPJ responses when appraising someone's merit.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlighted this finding as noteworthy. One stated 'the relationship between neural signal and behavioural merit sensitivity in TPJ is noteworthy' and another noted 'brain responses during merit inferences (merit - control) systematically covaried with participants' merit sensitivity scores in the rTPJ.' This finding was treated as a key contribution linking neural activity to behavioral parameters.

results.result: In the altruism task, participants were more generous to partners in high (vs. low) need, high (vs. low) merit, and unknown (vs. low) merit. Merit and need had independent effects on generosity with no significant interactions, and merit-induced and need-induced changes in generosity were uncorrelated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these behavioral findings without critique. One reviewer summarized that 'behaviour is indeed influenced, as expected, by the deservingness and the need of the shown people.' The independence of merit and need effects was accepted as part of the overall pattern of results showing that 'the conclusions of the paper are overall well supported by the data.'

results.result: A computational model of altruistic choice showed that self-related outcomes strongly guided choices, more than concern for others or fairness. When interacting with high (vs. low) merit partners, self-regard decreased while other-regard and fairness concerns increased. In high (vs. low) need settings, self-regard decreased and other-regard increased, but fairness concerns decreased.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the computational modeling of the altruism task. One noted 'the authors use sound and robust computational modelling approach for both tasks' and 'the methods are very solid with many supplementary analyses.' The model fit was accepted as adequate (R² = 0.33), and reviewers did not challenge the interpretation of how merit and need differentially affected attribute weights.

results.result: Merit bias predicted context-independent variance in overall other-regard during altruistic choice, biasing people toward prosocial actions. Merit sensitivity predicted merit-induced changes in generosity. These relationships held across tasks completed approximately 10 months apart, suggesting stable individual differences.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found the cross-task correlations 'impressive' and noted they 'suggest that the tasks are sensitive for important individual differences,' they consistently raised concerns about sample size. Multiple reviewers stated 'these are small samples' and 'the number of participants in the latter analyses are at the lower end.' One noted 'we cannot conclude much from absent relationships, where the likelihood of Type II error is high.' The editor concluded 'claims however would be stronger with a larger sample size.'

results.result: Merit sensitivity predicted context-sensitive discrimination in generosity toward high and low merit recipients by influencing both other-regard and self-regard during altruistic decision-making. Individuals with higher merit sensitivity showed larger discrimination in the value placed on others' wellbeing and self-interest when interacting with deserving versus undeserving people.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these findings as part of the overall pattern but expressed concerns about sample size for correlational analyses. One reviewer noted 'the number of participants in the latter analyses are at the lower end of the number of participants that are these days used for across-participant correlations.' While the findings were not directly challenged, the small sample size creates uncertainty about their robustness.

results.result: The context-sensitive perception-action link was associated with rTPJ activation. Both merit sensitivity and rTPJ responses independently predicted changes in other-regard during social choice approximately 10 months later. rTPJ responses during merit inferences predicted context-dependent changes in both other-regard and self-regard, above and beyond behavioral merit sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found this cross-task neural-behavioral correlation particularly impressive, with one stating 'the neural signal and aspects of the behaviour are correlated across subjects with the second task that is conducted much later. Such a correlation is very impressive.' However, they consistently noted sample size concerns, stating 'the number of participants in the latter analyses are at the lower end.' The editor emphasized that 'claims however would be stronger with a larger sample size.'

results.result: Variance in participants' need sensitivity did not reflect need-induced changes in generosity in the altruism task.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not explicitly discuss this null finding, but one noted that with small samples 'we cannot conclude much from absent relationships, where the likelihood of Type II error is high.' This suggests the null finding for need sensitivity should be interpreted cautiously given the sample size limitations.

results.result: The percentage of trials perceived by participants as depicting someone as deserving ranged from 33% to 81%, and the range for perceiving someone in need was 28–73%, showing substantial individual variability in social perceptions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these descriptive behavioral findings. They were accepted as part of the overall demonstration that the tasks successfully captured individual differences in social perception.

results.result: Methodological details including sample sizes (n=44 for social perception task, n=28 for altruism task, n=25 overlap), task timing (300 days average separation), exclusion criteria, and task parameters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently raised concerns about sample size. Multiple reviewers stated 'these are small samples,' 'sample size is quite small for study 2,' and 'the number of participants in the latter analyses are at the lower end.' The editor concluded 'claims however would be stronger with a larger sample size.' While the methods were otherwise praised as 'very solid,' the small sample size was a recurring concern.

results.result: The findings point toward stable, biologically based individual differences in perceptual processes related to abstract social concepts like merit, with potential implications for favoritism or discrimination in social settings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found the overall conclusions well-supported, with one stating 'the conclusions of the paper are overall well supported by the data.' The editor noted these are 'important findings' that 'stand out from other similar studies via some convincing demonstration of behavioural and neural relationships between two helping tasks.' However, the caveat about sample size applies to the strength of these broader conclusions.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on neural circuitry findings (C2, C21-C24, C61-C63). Both evaluations find the evidence strongly supported, with reviewers explicitly acknowledging the mentalizing network activation and inability to decode need vs merit judgments. OpenEval and peer reviewers treat these findings as key contributions demonstrating overlapping neural mechanisms.

Strong agreement on computational modeling approach (C3, C14-C20, C64). Both evaluations praise the modeling as thorough and well-executed. Peer reviewers note minor caveats about task simplicity and bias term interpretation, but these do not undermine acceptance. Both find the dual-mechanism model adequately supported.

Strong agreement on rTPJ-merit sensitivity correlation (C25, C26). Both evaluations highlight this brain-behavior relationship as noteworthy and well-supported. OpenEval additionally includes C7 (rTPJ link to altruism task), which peer reviewers address separately in R8 with sample size concerns.

Complete agreement on behavioral independence of merit and need effects (C28-C33, C67-C68). Both evaluations accept these findings without challenge. Peer reviewers acknowledge the expected influence of deservingness and need on behavior, treating the independence as well-supported by the data.

Strong agreement on computational mechanisms in altruism task (C34-C39, C65-C66). Both evaluations praise the modeling approach as sound and robust. The model fit (R²=0.33) and differential effects on attribute weights are accepted without challenge by both OpenEval and peer reviewers.

Divergent evaluations on temporal stability findings (C4, C40). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing substantial effect size (r=0.51) and temporal separation. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, finding correlations 'impressive' but consistently raising concerns about small sample size (n=25) and Type II error risk. Peer review includes C5, C70-C71 which OpenEval addresses separately in R7.

Divergent evaluations on merit bias and prosocial orientation (C5, C70-C71). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting the correlation between merit bias and other-regard (r=0.50). Peer reviewers group these claims with C4, C40 and rate as UNCERTAIN due to sample size concerns, though they find the cross-task correlations impressive.

Partial overlap on perception-action mechanisms (C6, C69). OpenEval groups these with C4, C40 in R6 and rates SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers address C6, C69 separately in R7 and rate UNCERTAIN due to sample size concerns for correlational analyses, though findings are not directly challenged.

Divergent evaluations on neural-behavioral prediction (C43, C44, C72). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing substantial explanatory power (R²=0.40) and independent contributions of both predictors. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, finding the cross-task correlation 'very impressive' but emphasizing sample size limitations. Peer review also includes C7, which OpenEval addresses in R3.

Agreement on uncertainty regarding need sensitivity null finding (C27). Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval questions whether null reflects true absence, insufficient power, or methodological limitations. Peer reviewers note that small samples preclude conclusions about absent relationships due to Type II error risk.

Partial agreement on descriptive behavioral data (C12, C13). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED while noting sample size limitations. Peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these findings without challenge as demonstrating individual differences. However, peer review does not address C46-C50 which OpenEval includes in R10.

Divergent evaluations on methodological details (C51-C60). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting these details support experimental validity. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, praising methods as 'very solid' but consistently raising concerns about small sample sizes (C45-C50). Peer review focuses on sample size issues while OpenEval emphasizes methodological rigor.

Qualified agreement on broad interpretive conclusions (C73, C74). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the correlational nature of fMRI data and that speculation about real-world implications requires caution. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, stating conclusions are 'overall well supported' and represent 'important findings,' though they note sample size caveats apply to strength of conclusions.

OpenEval addresses theoretical foundation and literature context (C1, C8-C11), rating as SUPPORTED but noting these are background claims rather than novel findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not separately evaluate these contextual claims.

Partial overlap on C7 (rTPJ activation predicting altruism behavior). OpenEval includes C7 in R3 with C25-C26 and rates SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers address C7 in R8 alongside C43-C44, C72 and rate UNCERTAIN due to sample size concerns for cross-task correlations.

Partial overlap on sample characteristics (C45-C50). OpenEval includes these in R10 with C12-C13 and rates SUPPORTED while noting sample size limitations. Peer reviewers include these in R11 with C51-C60 and rate UNCERTAIN, emphasizing that small sample sizes are a primary concern affecting interpretation.
